blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Physical Quantities: The Quantities which are used to describe the laws of physics and can be measured are called Physical Quantities

Fundamental or Base Quantities: The quantities which do not depend upon other quantities for their complete definition are known as fundamental or base quantities.

(1) Mass

(2) Length

(3) Time

(4) Temperature

(5) Current

(6) Luminous Intensity

(7) Amount of Substance

Derived Quantities: The quantities which can be expressed in terms of the fundamental quantities are known as derived quantities.

Example : Area, Force, Density, etc

Dimensions: Dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers (or exponents) to which the base quantities are raised to express that quantity.

Dimensional Formula: The dimensional formula of any physical quantity is that expression which represents how and which of the base quantities are included in that quantity.

It is written by enclosing the symbols for base quantities with appropriate powers in square brackets.

Mass = [M1L0T0]

Momentum = [M1L1T–1]

Force= [M1L1T–2]

Dimensional Equation: The equation obtained by equating a physical quantity with its dimensional formula is called a dimensional equation.

For example:

Length = [M0L1T0]

Only same physical quantities can be added or subtracted.

A + B = C – D

Dimensionless Quantities

Dimensionless Quantities are:

• Ratio of physical quantities with same dimensions.
    • All Mathematical constant.
    • All standard mathematical functions and their inputs.

(1) Conversion between System of Units :

Magnitude = numeric value (n) × unit (u) = constant

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{n}_1 \mathrm{u}_1=\mathrm{n}_2 \mathrm{u}_2 \\ & \mathrm{n}_2=\mathrm{n}_1\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}_1}{\mathrm{u}_2}\right) \end{aligned}$

So, if a quantity is represented by [Ma Lb Tc] then

$ \mathrm{n}_2=\mathrm{n}_1\left(\frac{\mathrm{M}_1}{\mathrm{M}_2}\right)^{\mathrm{a}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~L}_1}{\mathrm{~L}_2}\right)^{\mathrm{b}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~T}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_2}\right)^{\mathrm{c}}$

n1 = numerical value in I system

M1 = unit of mass in I system

n2 = numerical value in II system

M2 = unit of mass in II system

L1 = unit of length in I system

T1 = unit of time in I system

L2 = unit of length in II system

T2 = unit of time in II system

(2) To check the dimensional correctness of a given physical relation: If in a given relation, the terms on both the sides have the same dimensions, then the relation is dimensionally correct. This is known as the Principle of Homogeneity of Dimensions.

(3) To derive relationship between different physical quantities: Using the same principle of homogeneity of dimensions new relations among physical quantities can be derived if the dependent quantities are known.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Convert 2J to a system where unit of mass, length and time are 10g, 20m and 10s respectively?
blocks.prompt: Convert 2J to a system where unit of mass, length and time are 10g, 20m and 10s respectively?

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: It is known that the time of revolution T of a satellite around the earth depends on the universal gravitational constant G, the mass of the earth M, and the radius of the circular orbit R. Obtain an expression for T using dimensional analysis.
blocks.answer:
$\text { We have }[\mathrm{T}] \propto[\mathrm{G}]^{\mathrm{a}}[\mathrm{M}]^{\mathrm{b}}[\mathrm{R}]^{\mathrm{c}}$

$\Rightarrow[\mathrm{M}]^0[\mathrm{~L}]^0[\mathrm{~T}]^1=[\mathrm{M}]^{-\mathrm{a}}[\mathrm{~L}]^{3 \mathrm{a}}[\mathrm{T}]^{-2 \mathrm{a}} \times[\mathrm{M}]^{\mathrm{b}} \times[\mathrm{L}]^{\mathrm{c}}=[\mathrm{M}]^{\mathrm{b}-\mathrm{a}}[\mathrm{L}]^{\mathrm{c}+3 \mathrm{a}}[\mathrm{~T}]^{-2 \mathrm{a}}$

Comparing the exponents

$\text { For }[T]: 1=-2 a \Rightarrow a=-\frac{1}{2}$

$\text { For }[M]: 0=b-a \Rightarrow b=a=-\frac{1}{2}$

$\text { For }[L]: 0=c+3 a \Rightarrow c=-3 a=\frac{3}{2}$

$\text { Putting the values we get } T \propto G^{-1 / 2} M^{-1 / 2} R^{3 / 2} \Rightarrow T \propto \sqrt{\frac{R^3}{G M}}$
blocks.prompt: It is known that the time of revolution T of a satellite around the earth depends on the universal gravitational constant G, the mass of the earth M, and the radius of the circular orbit R. Obtain an expression for T using dimensional analysis.

modules.name: Significant Figures, Rounding off and Order of magnitude

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Significant Figures or Digits:

• Significant figures (SF) in a measurement are the figures or digits that are known with certainty plus one that is uncertain (i.e. Last digit).

Rules to find out the number of significant figures

I Rule : All the non-zero digits are significant

e.g. 1984 has 4 SF.

II Rule : All the zeros between two non-zero digits are significant.

e.g. 10806 has 5 SF.

III Rule : All the zeros to the left of first non-zero digit are not significant.

e.g.00108 has 3 SF.

IV Rule : If the number is less than 1, zeros on the right of the decimal point and to the left of the first non-zero digit are not significant.

e.g. 0.002308 has 4 SF.

V Rule : The trailing zeros (zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit) in a number with a decimal point are significant.

e.g. 01.080 has 4 SF.

VI Rule :  The trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point may not be significant

e.g. 010100 has 3 SF.

VII Rule : When the number is expressed in exponential form, the exponential term does not affect the number of S.F.

For example, in x = 12.3 = 1.23 × 101 = 0.123 × 102

= 0.0123 × 103 = 123 × 10 –1 each term has 3 SF only.

Rounding off: To represent the result of any computation containing more than one uncertain digit, it is rounded off to appropriate number of significant figures.

Rules for rounding off the numbers:

I Rule : If the digit to be rounded off is more than 5, then the preceding digit is increased by one.

$\text { e.g. } 6.87 \approx 6.9$

II Rule : If the digit to be rounded off is less than 5, then the preceding digit is left unchanged.

$\text { e.g. } 3.94 \approx 3.9$

III Rule : If the digit to be rounded off is 5 then the preceding digit is increased by one if it is odd and is left unchanged if it is even

$\text { e.g. } 14.35 \approx 14.4 \text { and } 14.45 \approx 14.4$

Rules for arithmetical operations with significant figures

I Rule : In addition, or subtraction the number of decimal places in the result should be equal to the number of decimal places of that term in the operation which contain lesser number of decimal places.

e.g. 12.587 – 12.5 = 0.087 = 0.1 ( second term contain lesser i.e. one decimal place)

II Rule : In multiplication or division, the number of SF in the product or quotient is same as the smallest number of SF in any of the factors.

e.g. 2.4 × 3.65 = 8.8

Order of Magnitude: Order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of 10 required to represent that quantity. This power is determined after rounding off the value of the quantity properly. For rounding off, the last digit is simply ignored if it is less than 5 and, is increased by one if it is 5 or more than 5.

$0.5 \leq \mathrm{N} / 10 ^{x}<5$ then $x$ is order of magnitude.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: The length, breadth and thickness of a metal sheet are 4.234 m, 1.005 m and 2.01 cm respectively. Give the area and volume of the sheet to correct number of significant figures.
blocks.answer:
$\text { length }(\ell)=4.234 \mathrm{~m} \quad \text { breadth }(\mathrm{b})=1.005 \mathrm{~m} \quad \text { thickness }(\mathrm{t})=2.01 \mathrm{~cm}=2.01 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}$

Therefore, area of the sheet

$\begin{aligned} & =2(\ell \times \mathrm{b}+\mathrm{b} \times \mathrm{t}+\mathrm{t} \times \ell) \mid \\ & =2(4.234 \times 1.005+1.005 \times 0.0201+0.0201 \times 4.234) \mathrm{m}^2 \\ & =2(4.3604739) \mathrm{m}^2=8.720978 \mathrm{~m}^2 \end{aligned}$

Since area can contain a maximum of 3 SF therefore, rounding off, we get:

$\text { : Area }=8.72 \mathrm{~m}^2$

$\text { Likewise, volume }=\ell \times \mathrm{b} \times \mathrm{t}=4.234 \times 1.005 \times 0.0201 \mathrm{~m}^3=0.0855289 \mathrm{~m}^3$

Since volume can contain 3 SF, therefore after rounding off, we get:

$\text { Volume }=0.0855 \mathrm{~m}^3$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Failing to recognize how many significant figures are appropriate for the result of a calculation, especially when rounding.
  • Miscounting zeros when determining the number of significant figures.
  • Rounding incorrectly when adding or subtracting values with different decimal places.
  • Not applying significant figures correctly when working with numbers in scientific notation.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Errors in Measurement:

The difference between the true value and the measured value of a quantity is known as the error in the measurement.

Error = True value – Measured value

Types of Errors

1. Systematic Errors:

Systematic errors are the errors whose causes are known. They can be either positive or negative. Due to the known causes these errors can be minimized. Systematic errors can further be classified into three categories:

(1) Instrumental errors

(2) Environmental errors

(3) Observational errors

2. Random Errors:

These errors are due to unknown causes. Therefore, they occur irregularly and are variable in magnitude and sign. The causes of these errors are not known precisely, they cannot be eliminated completely.

3. Gross Errors:

Gross errors arise due to human carelessness and mistakes in taking reading or calculating and recording the measurement results.

Representation of Errors

1. Absolute Error$(\Delta a )$ :

The difference between the true value and the individual measured value of the quantity is called the absolute error of the measurement.

Absolute Error = True Value – Measured Value

$\Delta a = a_T - a$

2.Mean Absolute Error$(\Delta a)_m$ :

The arithmetic mean of all the absolute errors(magnitudes) is defined as the final or mean absolute error.

Mean Absolute Error=$(\Delta a)_m = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^n |\Delta a_i|$

3.Relative Or Fractional Error:

It is defined as the ratio of the mean absolute error to the true value or the mean value of the quantity measured.

$\text{Relative Error} = \dfrac{\text{Mean Absolute Error}}{\text{True Value}}$=$\frac{(\Delta a)_m}{a_m}$

Percentage Error:

When the relative error is expressed in percentage, it is known as percentage error.

Percentage Error = Relative Error × 100%

$\text{Percentage Error} = \dfrac{\text{Mean Absolute Error}}{\text{True Value}} \times100\%
$

Least Count:

It is the smallest value of a physical quantity that can be measured accurately by an instrument.

Least Count Error:

This is related to the resolution of the measuring instrument.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Propagation of Errors

Rule 1: -

Addition or Subtraction of Quantities: The maximum absolute error in the sum or difference of the two quantities is equal to the sum of the absolute errors in the individual quantities.

If X = A + B or X = A – B and  $\pm \Delta A$ and  $\pm \Delta B$ represent the absolute errors in A and B respectively, then the maximum absolute error in X is  $\Delta X = \Delta A + \Delta B$

Rule 2: -

Multiplication or Division of Quantities: The maximum fractional or relative error in the product or quotient of quantities is equal to the sum of the fractional or relative errors in the individual quantities.

If  $X = AB$ or $X = \dfrac{A}{B}$  Then $\dfrac{\Delta X}{X} = \pm \left( \dfrac{\Delta A}{A} + \dfrac{\Delta B}{B} \right)$

Rule 3: -

The maximum fractional error in a quantity raised to a power (n) is n times the fractional error in the quantity itself,

(1) If $X = A^n \quad \text{then} \quad \frac{\Delta X}{X} = n \left( \frac{\Delta A}{A} \right)$

(2) If $X = A^p B^q C^r \quad \text{then} \quad \frac{\Delta X}{X} = \left[ p \left( \frac{\Delta A}{A} \right) + q \left( \frac{\Delta B}{B} \right) + r \left( \frac{\Delta C}{C} \right) \right]$

(3) If$X = \frac{A^p B^q}{C^r} \quad \text{then} \quad \frac{\Delta X}{X} = \left[ p \left( \frac{\Delta A}{A} \right) + q \left( \frac{\Delta B}{B} \right) + r \left( \frac{\Delta C}{C} \right) \right]$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
The initial and final temperatures of water as recorded by an observer are

$(40.6 \pm 0.2)^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { and }(78.3 \pm 0.3)^{\circ} \mathrm{C} .$Calculate the rise in temperature with proper error limits.
blocks.answer:
Answer  $\text { Rise in temperature }=(37.7 \pm 0.5)^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\text { Given } \theta_1=(40.6 \pm 0.2)^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { and } \theta_2=(78.3 \pm 0.3)^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

Rise in temp

$\theta=\theta_2-\theta_1=78.3-40.6=37.7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\Delta \theta= \pm\left(\Delta \theta_1+\Delta \theta_2\right)= \pm(0.2+0.3)= \pm 0.5 \mathrm{C}$

Rise in temperature=$(37.7 \pm 0.5)^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
A thin copper wire of length L increases in length by 2% when heated from T1 to T2. If a copper cube having side 10 L is heated from T1 to T2 what will be the percentage change in

(i) Area of one face of the cube and.

(ii) Volume of the cube.
blocks.answer:
Answer Area= $4 \%$     Change in Volume =$6 \%$

$\text { (i) } \quad \text { Area } A=10 \mathrm{~L} \times 10 \mathrm{~L}=100 \mathrm{~L}^2 \Rightarrow A \propto \mathrm{~L}^2$

$\% \text { change in area }=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{~A}} \times 100=2 \times \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{~L}} \times 100=2 \times 2 \%=4 \%$

$\text { (ii) Volume } \mathrm{V}=10 \mathrm{~L} \times 10 \mathrm{~L} \times 10 \mathrm{~L}=1000 \mathrm{~L}^3 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~V} \propto \mathrm{~L}^3$

$\% \text { change in volume }=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{~V}} \times 100=3 \frac{\Delta \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{~L}} \times 100 =3 \times 2 \%=6 \%$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Vernier Callipers: A measuring device that is used for the measurement of linear dimensions. It is also used for the measurement of diameters of round objects with the help of the measuring jaws.

Least Count of Vernier Callipers:

$L. C.=1 \mathrm{MSD}-1 V S D$

Measurement with Vernier Calliper

READING = (Main Scale Reading) + (Vernier Scale Reading)

READING = $M S D \times L C \text { of } M S$ + (VS Coincided division with any MSD × LC)

Zero Error: If the zero marking of main scale and Vernier scale do not coincide when no object than, necessary correction has to be made for this error which is known as zero error of the instrument.

1. Positive Zero Error: If the zero of the Vernier scale is to the right of the zero of then main scale the zero error is said to be positive. The zero error is always subtracted from the reading to get the corrected value.

READING = (Main Scale Reading) + (Vernier Scale Reading) – ZE

Positive zero error = VS Coincided division with MS × LC of VS

2.Negative Zero Error: If the zero of the Vernier scale is to the left of the zero of the main scale the zero error is said to be negative. The zero error is always subtracted from the reading to get the corrected value.

Negative Zero Error Correction

Negative zero error = –(Total VSD – VS Coincided division with  MS) × LC of VS

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: If the jaws of the vernier callipers are in contact with each other, then determine the zero error of the vernier calliper if the VSD is 3. (take its least count as 0.1mm)
blocks.answer:
Answer $0.3 mm$

Given: The jaws of the vernier calliper are in contact with each other.

Therefore, the least count of the vernier calliper is given as:

LC = 0.1 mm

The vernier scale reading, VSR = 3

$\text { Therefore, Zero error }=\mathrm{VSR} \times \mathrm{LC}=3 \times 0.1=0.3 \mathrm{~mm}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ensure the Vernier scale is exactly aligned with the main scale to avoid parallax errors.
  • Before measurement, always check if the instrument is calibrated to zero and adjust if necessary.
  • Over-tightening the locking screw when adjusting the callipers can lead to slight deformation, affecting accuracy.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Screw Gauge: For precise measurement of spherical or a cylindrical object, a screw gauge is the best instrument.

Pitch of Screw Gauge: The pitch of the instrument is the distance between two consecutive threads of the screw which is equal to the distance moved by the screw due to one complete rotation of the cap.

Least Count of Screw Gauge

The minimum (or least) measurement (or count) of length is equal to one division on the main scale (which is equal to pitch) divided by the total circle scale divisions.

• Pitch of screw gauge = P
    • Number of division on circular scale = N

$\text { Least count of screw gauge }=\dfrac{\text { Pitch }(\mathrm{P})}{\text { Total no. of divisions on the circular scale }(\mathrm{N})}$

Measurement by Screw Gauge: The formula for measuring the length is,     L = (n × pitch) + (f × least count)

Where, n = main scale division; f = Circular scale division coincided with base lin

Zero Error in Screw Gauge: If there is no object between the studs (i.e. studs are in contact), If the zero marking on circular scale do not coincide with main scale base line.

Calculation of zero error for screw gauge: -

Positive zero error = CS Coincided division with MS × LC

Negative zero error = –(Total CSD – CS Coincided division with MS base line ) × LC of CS

Correct reading = (Reading) – (zero error)

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Before using the screw gauge, it should be checked for zero error.
  • The object being measured should be perpendicular to the anvil and spindle of the screw gauge.
  • Parallax error occurs if the scale is viewed from an angle rather than straight on.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A spherometer has 50 equal divisions marked along the periphery of its disc, and one full rotation of the disc advances on the main scale by 0.01 cm. Find the least count of the system.
blocks.answer:
Answer  $2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}$

Given, Pitch = 0.01 cm

$\text { Least count }=\frac{\text { Pitch }}{\text { Total no. of divisions on the the circular scale }}$

L.C. = $\dfrac{0.01}{50} \mathrm{~cm}=2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}$
blocks.prompt: A spherometer has 50 equal divisions marked along the periphery of its disc, and one full rotation of the disc advances on the main scale by 0.01 cm. Find the least count of the system.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: The pitch of screw gauge is 1 mm and there are 100 divisions on the circular scale. In measuring the diameter of a sphere there are 6 divisions on the linear scale and forty division on circular scale coincide with the reference line. Find the diameter of the sphere.
blocks.answer:
Answer $6.40 mm$

Least count of the screw gauge is L.C = pitch / number of circular scale divisions = 1/100 = 0.01mm

Main scale reading (MSR) = 6 × 1mm = 6mm

Circular scale reading (CSR) = 40 × 0.01mm

$\text { Diameter of the sphere }=\text { MSR }+(\mathrm{CSR})=6+(40 \times 0.01)=6.40 \mathrm{~mm}$

$\text { e.g. } 14.35 \approx 14.4 \text { and } 14.45 \approx 14.4$

I Rule : In addition, or subtraction the number of decimal places in the result should be equal to the number of decimal places of that term in the operation which contain lesser number of decimal places.

e.g. 12.587 – 12.5 = 0.087 = 0.1 ( second term contain lesser i.e. one decimal place)

II Rule : In multiplication or division, the number of SF in the product or quotient is same as the smallest number of SF in any of the factors.

e.g. 2.4 × 3.65 = 8.8

Order of Magnitude: Order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of 10 required to represent that quantity. This power is determined after rounding off the value of the quantity properly. For rounding off, the last digit is simply ignored if it is less than 5 and, is increased by one if it is 5 or more than 5.

$0.5 \leq \mathrm{N} / 10 ^{x}<5$ then $x$ is order of magnitude.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Errors in Measurement:

The difference between the true value and the measured value of a quantity is known as the error in the measurement.

Error = True value – Measured value

Types of Errors

1. Systematic Errors:

Systematic errors are the errors whose causes are known. They can be either positive or negative. Due to the known causes these errors can be minimized. Systematic errors can further be classified into three categories:

(1) Instrumental errors

(2) Environmental errors

(3) Observational errors

2. Random Errors:

These errors are due to unknown causes. Therefore, they occur irregularly and are variable in magnitude and sign. The causes of these errors are not known precisely, they cannot be eliminated completely.

3. Gross Errors:

Gross errors arise due to human carelessness and mistakes in taking reading or calculating and recording the measurement results.

Representation of Errors

1. Absolute Error$(\Delta a )$ :

The difference between the true value and the individual measured value of the quantity is called the absolute error of the measurement.

Absolute Error = True Value – Measured Value

$\Delta a = a_T - a$

2.Mean Absolute Error$(\Delta a)_m$ :

The arithmetic mean of all the absolute errors(magnitudes) is defined as the final or mean absolute error.

Mean Absolute Error=$(\Delta a)_m = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^n |\Delta a_i|$

3.Relative Or Fractional Error:

It is defined as the ratio of the mean absolute error to the true value or the mean value of the quantity measured.

$\text{Relative Error} = \dfrac{\text{Mean Absolute Error}}{\text{True Value}}$=$\frac{(\Delta a)_m}{a_m}$

Percentage Error:

When the relative error is expressed in percentage, it is known as percentage error.

Percentage Error = Relative Error × 100%

$\text{Percentage Error} = \dfrac{\text{Mean Absolute Error}}{\text{True Value}} \times100\%
$

Least Count:

It is the smallest value of a physical quantity that can be measured accurately by an instrument.

Least Count Error:

This is related to the resolution of the measuring instrument.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Propagation of Errors

Rule 1: -

Addition or Subtraction of Quantities: The maximum absolute error in the sum or difference of the two quantities is equal to the sum of the absolute errors in the individual quantities.

If X = A + B or X = A – B and  $\pm \Delta A$ and  $\pm \Delta B$ represent the absolute errors in A and B respectively, then the maximum absolute error in X is  $\Delta X = \Delta A + \Delta B$

Rule 2: -

Multiplication or Division of Quantities: The maximum fractional or relative error in the product or quotient of quantities is equal to the sum of the fractional or relative errors in the individual quantities.

If  $X = AB$ or $X = \dfrac{A}{B}$  Then $\dfrac{\Delta X}{X} = \pm \left( \dfrac{\Delta A}{A} + \dfrac{\Delta B}{B} \right)$

Rule 3: -

The maximum fractional error in a quantity raised to a power (n) is n times the fractional error in the quantity itself,

(1) If $X = A^n \quad \text{then} \quad \frac{\Delta X}{X} = n \left( \frac{\Delta A}{A} \right)$

(2) If $X = A^p B^q C^r \quad \text{then} \quad \frac{\Delta X}{X} = \left[ p \left( \frac{\Delta A}{A} \right) + q \left( \frac{\Delta B}{B} \right) + r \left( \frac{\Delta C}{C} \right) \right]$

(3) If$X = \frac{A^p B^q}{C^r} \quad \text{then} \quad \frac{\Delta X}{X} = \left[ p \left( \frac{\Delta A}{A} \right) + q \left( \frac{\Delta B}{B} \right) + r \left( \frac{\Delta C}{C} \right) \right]$
